## Guided Tutorial 12.1: Reconciling the Populations, Tracing the Ledger, and Testing Cutoff

**Context and objective.** Before testing any process, the audit team must know that the ledger and its populations can be relied on. In this tutorial, you will reconcile the journal entries and the manufacturing payroll to the ledger, trace postings to their documents and documents to their postings, and explain the exceptions you find. You will then test the cutoff of revenue and of payroll at each year-end.

**Prerequisites.** Complete the tutorials of the earlier Part III chapters, and open CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite in DB Browser for SQLite on the **Execute SQL** tab. If Chapter11.sql is still open in the editor, click **New tab** (Ctrl+T) for an empty editor tab. Start a new script for the audit query library with the header comment below, with your own name and the date, and click **Save SQL file** to save it as `Audit.sql` beside your working copy. As in Chapters 9 to 11, type each test at the end of the script, under its comment, and run it by selecting it. The first line of each comment names the test, and the second states its population and the result expected if the controls worked. If you start here, you need only the working copy, made as Step 1 of Tutorial 9.1 describes.

```sql
/* Audit.sql: tests of the records behind the manufacturing variance
   Database: CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite (a copy of CharlesRiver.sqlite)
   Prepared by: your name, date; reviewed by: name, date
   Checks: listed at the end of Tutorial 12.3 */
```

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Reconcile the journal entries to the ledger.** Scalar subqueries in the SELECT list put the totals of two tables side by side, as in Tutorial 10.2.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L1: journal entries against the ledger
   -- Population: all journal entries; expected: counts and totals agree
   SELECT
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM JournalEntry) AS Entries,
       (SELECT ROUND(SUM(TotalAmount), 2) FROM JournalEntry) AS EntryTotal,
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT SourceDocumentID) FROM GLEntry
           WHERE SourceDocumentType = 'JournalEntry') AS PostedEntries,
       (SELECT ROUND(SUM(Debit), 2) FROM GLEntry
           WHERE SourceDocumentType = 'JournalEntry') AS PostedDebits;
   ```

b. Compare the first two columns with the last two.

The number of entries and their total agree with the entries and the debits posted to the ledger, as Tutorial 8.3 found in Excel. Agreement of counts and totals shows that the population is complete with respect to the ledger; the trace of Step 3 then tests the postings one by one.

**Step 2. Reconcile the manufacturing payroll to the ledger.** The payroll registers state what each employee was paid and what the company paid on top, and GLEntry records the cost center of each posting.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L2: manufacturing payroll against the ledger
   -- Population: Manufacturing registers; expected: no difference
   SELECT reg.FiscalYear, reg.RegisterCost, gl.LedgerCost,
       ROUND(reg.RegisterCost - gl.LedgerCost, 2) AS Difference
   FROM (
       SELECT pp.FiscalYear,
           ROUND(SUM(pr.GrossPay + pr.EmployerPayrollTax
               + pr.EmployerBenefits), 2) AS RegisterCost
       FROM PayrollRegister AS pr
           INNER JOIN PayrollPeriod AS pp
               ON pp.PayrollPeriodID = pr.PayrollPeriodID
           INNER JOIN CostCenter AS cc ON cc.CostCenterID = pr.CostCenterID
       WHERE cc.CostCenterName = 'Manufacturing'
       GROUP BY pp.FiscalYear
   ) AS reg
       INNER JOIN (
           SELECT gl.FiscalYear, ROUND(SUM(gl.Debit), 2) AS LedgerCost
           FROM GLEntry AS gl
               INNER JOIN CostCenter AS cc
                   ON cc.CostCenterID = gl.CostCenterID
           WHERE gl.SourceDocumentType = 'PayrollSummary'
               AND cc.CostCenterName = 'Manufacturing'
           GROUP BY gl.FiscalYear
       ) AS gl ON gl.FiscalYear = reg.FiscalYear
   ORDER BY reg.FiscalYear;
   ```

b. Read the Difference column.

The registers of the manufacturing cost center agree with the ledger's payroll postings to the cent in each year. The ledger side counts the postings to every account, not only account 1090: the manufacturing part of the first payroll of 2024 was posted to the variance account, as Tutorial 11.2 noted, so a comparison with account 1090 alone would differ in that year. Both sides record payroll on its pay date, so the test shows that the registers are complete with respect to the ledger. It cannot show whether wages earned but not yet paid were recorded, the question of Steps 7 and 8.

**Step 3. List the trace exceptions in both directions.** Each test is an anti-join, and UNION ALL stacks their results into one list, labeled by test.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L3: postings and documents traced both ways
   -- Population: four document types; expected: no rows
   SELECT 'Posting with no payroll payment' AS Test,
       gl.GLEntryID AS RecordID, gl.PostingDate AS RecordDate,
       gl.Debit + gl.Credit AS Amount
   FROM GLEntry AS gl
       LEFT JOIN PayrollPayment AS pp
           ON pp.PayrollPaymentID = gl.SourceDocumentID
   WHERE gl.SourceDocumentType = 'PayrollPayment'
       AND pp.PayrollPaymentID IS NULL
   UNION ALL
   SELECT 'Posting with no supplier payment', gl.GLEntryID,
       gl.PostingDate, gl.Debit + gl.Credit
   FROM GLEntry AS gl
       LEFT JOIN DisbursementPayment AS dp
           ON dp.DisbursementID = gl.SourceDocumentID
   WHERE gl.SourceDocumentType = 'DisbursementPayment'
       AND dp.DisbursementID IS NULL
   UNION ALL
   SELECT 'Sales invoice never posted', si.SalesInvoiceID,
       si.InvoiceDate, si.GrandTotal
   FROM SalesInvoice AS si
       LEFT JOIN GLEntry AS gl ON gl.SourceDocumentType = 'SalesInvoice'
           AND gl.SourceDocumentID = si.SalesInvoiceID
   WHERE gl.GLEntryID IS NULL
   UNION ALL
   SELECT 'Supplier invoice never posted', pi.PurchaseInvoiceID,
       pi.InvoiceDate, pi.GrandTotal
   FROM PurchaseInvoice AS pi
       LEFT JOIN GLEntry AS gl ON gl.SourceDocumentType = 'PurchaseInvoice'
           AND gl.SourceDocumentID = pi.PurchaseInvoiceID
   WHERE gl.GLEntryID IS NULL;
   ```

b. Read the Test column of each row in the result.

The result, shown in @fig-12-02, holds six rows, all from the first test: the postings that Exercise 10.5 found. Six ledger rows record payroll payments that do not exist in the PayrollPayment table, three pairs, each a debit to accrued payroll and a credit to cash, in January of each year. The other three tests return no rows. Every supplier payment in the ledger has its document, and every sales and supplier invoice was posted.

![The Trace Exceptions in One List.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-02-trace-exceptions.svg){#fig-12-02 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Audit.sql, shows the start of a test that combines four anti-joins with UNION ALL: ledger postings with no payroll payment, ledger postings with no supplier payment, sales invoices never posted, and supplier invoices never posted. The result grid holds six rows, all labeled Posting with no payroll payment, three pairs of equal amounts dated in January 2024, January 2025, and January 2026. The Test column is outlined."}

**Step 4. Explain the six postings.** A payroll payment normally carries the same ID as the payroll register it pays, so the missing payments point to their registers. CostCenter appears twice in the test, as ec for the employee's own cost center and as rc for the register's, so that each row can show both.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L4: approved registers with no payment
   -- Population: all payroll registers; expected: no rows
   SELECT pr.PayrollRegisterID, e.JobTitle,
       ec.CostCenterName AS EmployeeCenter,
       rc.CostCenterName AS RegisterCenter, e.TerminationDate,
       pp.PayDate, pr.GrossPay, pr.NetPay, pr.Status
   FROM PayrollRegister AS pr
       INNER JOIN PayrollPeriod AS pp
           ON pp.PayrollPeriodID = pr.PayrollPeriodID
       INNER JOIN Employee AS e ON e.EmployeeID = pr.EmployeeID
       INNER JOIN CostCenter AS ec ON ec.CostCenterID = e.CostCenterID
       INNER JOIN CostCenter AS rc ON rc.CostCenterID = pr.CostCenterID
       LEFT JOIN PayrollPayment AS pay
           ON pay.PayrollRegisterID = pr.PayrollRegisterID
   WHERE pay.PayrollPaymentID IS NULL;
   ```

b. Compare the register IDs and net pay with the SourceDocumentID and amounts of the six postings.
c. Compare each register's cost center with its employee's.

Three approved registers have no payment record, and their IDs and net pay match the six postings: the ledger recorded the cash, but the payment documents are missing. The first register pays the chief executive officer. The other two pay an Account Executive of the Sales cost center, terminated in April 2024, in January 2025 and January 2026, and they are charged to the Executive cost center at the same gross pay as the chief executive's register. A credit to cash does not say who received the money, so the bank records must confirm the payee. Exercise 12.5 follows the employee further.

**Step 5. Test the cutoff of revenue.** Revenue belongs to the fiscal year in which the goods were delivered, so the test compares each invoice's posting date with the delivery date of the shipments it bills, and uses the invoice date as a second check. Read the test from the top: Shipped finds the first shipment date and the last delivery date of the goods each invoice bills, Posted finds the date on which each invoice was posted, Classified gives each invoice a finding with CASE, and the final query counts the exceptions.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L5: revenue posted in the year of delivery
   -- Population: all sales invoices; expected: no rows
   WITH Shipped AS (
       SELECT sil.SalesInvoiceID, MIN(s.ShipmentDate) AS ShipmentDate,
           MAX(s.DeliveryDate) AS DeliveryDate
       FROM SalesInvoiceLine AS sil
           INNER JOIN ShipmentLine AS sl
               ON sl.ShipmentLineID = sil.ShipmentLineID
           INNER JOIN Shipment AS s ON s.ShipmentID = sl.ShipmentID
       GROUP BY sil.SalesInvoiceID
   ),
   Posted AS (
       SELECT SourceDocumentID AS SalesInvoiceID,
           MIN(PostingDate) AS PostingDate
       FROM GLEntry
       WHERE SourceDocumentType = 'SalesInvoice'
       GROUP BY SourceDocumentID
   ),
   Classified AS (
       SELECT si.SubTotal,
           strftime('%Y', sh.DeliveryDate) AS DeliveryYear,
           CASE
               WHEN strftime('%Y', p.PostingDate)
                       <> strftime('%Y', sh.DeliveryDate)
                   THEN 'Revenue posted in another year'
               WHEN si.InvoiceDate < sh.ShipmentDate
                   THEN 'Invoice dated before shipment'
               ELSE 'In the year of delivery'
           END AS Finding
       FROM SalesInvoice AS si
           INNER JOIN Shipped AS sh
               ON sh.SalesInvoiceID = si.SalesInvoiceID
           INNER JOIN Posted AS p ON p.SalesInvoiceID = si.SalesInvoiceID
   )
   SELECT Finding, DeliveryYear, COUNT(*) AS Invoices,
       ROUND(SUM(SubTotal), 2) AS SubTotal
   FROM Classified
   WHERE Finding <> 'In the year of delivery'
   GROUP BY Finding, DeliveryYear
   ORDER BY Finding, DeliveryYear;
   ```

b. Read the rows of each finding.

The result, shown in @fig-12-03, has two findings. More than twenty invoices for goods delivered in December were invoiced and posted in January, so their revenue was recorded in the next fiscal year, while the cost of the goods was recorded when they shipped. Eight invoices are dated before their shipment, the kind of error that Tutorial 2.1 and Exercise 5.2 found; Exercise 12.1 lists them. The eight were posted in the year of delivery, so they are failures in the dating of invoices, not in the posting of revenue.

![Revenue Posted Outside the Year of Delivery.](/visuals/svg/fig-12-03-revenue-cutoff.svg){#fig-12-03 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Audit.sql, is scrolled to the part of a test that classifies each sales invoice with CASE: revenue posted in another year than the delivery of its goods, invoice dated before shipment, or in the year of delivery, and counts the exceptions by finding and delivery year. The result has five rows: invoices dated before shipment in each of the three years, and invoices whose revenue was posted in another year for deliveries of 2024 and 2025. The rows of revenue posted in another year are outlined."}

**Step 6. Find the shipments never invoiced.** An anti-join from the shipment lines to the invoice lines finds the goods that were shipped but not billed.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L6: shipments never invoiced
   -- Population: all shipment lines; expected: no rows
   SELECT s.ShipmentNumber, s.ShipmentDate, s.DeliveryDate,
       ROUND(sl.ExtendedStandardCost, 2) AS StandardCost,
       ROUND(sl.QuantityShipped * sol.UnitPrice * (1 - sol.Discount), 2)
           AS SalesValue
   FROM ShipmentLine AS sl
       INNER JOIN Shipment AS s ON s.ShipmentID = sl.ShipmentID
       INNER JOIN SalesOrderLine AS sol
           ON sol.SalesOrderLineID = sl.SalesOrderLineID
       LEFT JOIN SalesInvoiceLine AS sil
           ON sil.ShipmentLineID = sl.ShipmentLineID
   WHERE sil.SalesInvoiceLineID IS NULL
   ORDER BY s.ShipmentDate;
   ```

b. Read the dates and the two values of each row.

A handful of shipment lines of December 2026 have no invoice by the end of the data. Their cost is in the ledger at the year-end, and their revenue is not, the same timing as the invoices of Step 5. Exercise 12.1 measures the effect of both on each year.

**Step 7. List the pay periods that cross a year-end.** Wages belong to the period in which the work was done, but, as Tutorial 11.2 found, Charles River records payroll on its pay date, so a period whose work begins in one fiscal year and is paid in the next moves cost between the years.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L7: pay periods that cross a year-end
   -- Population: all pay periods; expected: every period processed
   SELECT pp.PeriodNumber, pp.PeriodStartDate, pp.PeriodEndDate,
       pp.PayDate, pp.Status, COALESCE(reg.Registers, 0) AS Registers,
       reg.PayrollCost
   FROM PayrollPeriod AS pp
       LEFT JOIN (
           SELECT PayrollPeriodID, COUNT(*) AS Registers,
               ROUND(SUM(GrossPay + EmployerPayrollTax
                   + EmployerBenefits), 2) AS PayrollCost
           FROM PayrollRegister
           GROUP BY PayrollPeriodID
       ) AS reg ON reg.PayrollPeriodID = pp.PayrollPeriodID
   WHERE strftime('%Y', pp.PeriodStartDate) <> strftime('%Y', pp.PayDate)
   ORDER BY pp.PeriodStartDate;
   ```

b. Read the dates, the Status, and the PayrollCost of each period.

At each year-end, the work of the last weeks of December was paid, and recorded, in January of the next fiscal year. At the end of fiscal 2026, the last two periods are still Open, with no registers, so the wages of late December 2026 are recorded nowhere.

**Step 8. Look for an accrual of the unpaid wages.** An accrual at the year-end would record the wages earned but not yet paid in account 2030 Accrued Payroll.

a. Type and run the test below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 12.1, test L8: accrued payroll at the year-end
   -- Population: account 2030 to 2026-12-31; expected: unpaid wages
   SELECT gl.SourceDocumentType, COUNT(*) AS Postings,
       ROUND(SUM(gl.Credit) - SUM(gl.Debit), 2) AS Balance
   FROM GLEntry AS gl
       INNER JOIN Account AS a ON a.AccountID = gl.AccountID
   WHERE a.AccountNumber = 2030 AND gl.PostingDate <= '2026-12-31'
   GROUP BY gl.SourceDocumentType;
   ```

b. Read the Balance of each source.

The balance of account 2030 is the opening entry of 2024, and the payroll summaries and payments net to zero, so no entry ever accrued the wages earned but not yet paid at a year-end. Each year's payroll cost follows its pay dates, and the liability at each year-end is understated by a little more than one pay period's payroll, a few hundred thousand dollars. Exercise 12.1 estimates the amounts.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the journal entries and the manufacturing payroll reconcile to the ledger to the cent;
- the combined trace returns six postings with no payroll payment and nothing else;
- the six postings match three approved registers without payments, two of them for a terminated employee, charged to the Executive cost center;
- the revenue of December deliveries invoiced in January was posted in the next fiscal year, and a few December 2026 shipments were never invoiced;
- no entry accrues the wages of late December at any year-end;
- Audit.sql holds the header and the eight tests of this tutorial, each under its comment.

The ledger is reliable as a whole: its populations reconcile, and nearly every posting traces to a document and back. Its weakness is timing. Revenue and payroll are recorded when they are invoiced and paid, not when they are earned, so each year-end is misstated by the transactions on either side of it, and the wages of each December's last weeks, manufacturing wages among them, are charged to the next year.
